strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting question: whether search can be entirely eliminated from board-game RL, extending the line of work that reduces MCTS dependence (Gumbel AlphaZero, Muesli) to its 'zero-search limit'. The empirical demonstration that a model-free method can match or beat AlphaZero-family methods under matched simulator budgets is a notable and useful result for a domain long assumed to require search.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for an RL paper: five environments plus 19x19 Go, an ablation isolating each of the three components (Table 2/Figure 6), a 27-point hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Appendix D), tuning of AlphaZero rollout counts so the baselines are given a fair chance (Appendix G), test-time search scaling and wall-clock inference-time verification (Appendix H), head-to-head matches against external engines (Pachi, GnuGo, Appendix I), and a small-game analysis confirming convergence to the quantal response equilibrium (Appendix L).

Baseline credibility is explicitly addressed: the authors justify the Pgx AlphaZero implementation against selection criteria and run a cross-implementation tournament against alpha-zero-general (Appendix F), which preempts the most obvious objection about baseline strength.

The method is clearly presented: the regularized policy optimization objective, its analytic solution (with a correct Lagrangian derivation in Appendix A), the λ-return targets with an empirical bias-variance motivation (Figure 4), and a complete pseudocode (Algorithm 1). Hyperparameters are unified across all five games, supporting the claim that no per-game tuning is needed.

Limitations are handled honestly: the paper explicitly concedes that efficiency does not imply superior asymptotic performance (corroborated by Appendix G.3 showing AlphaZero catches up at 3,200-4,000M evaluations) and that Elo-style comparisons are unreliable in their setting.

Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: implementation details (ResNet sizes, batch sizes, optimizers, thread counts, budget accounting), computational requirements (~2,000 A100 GPU hours), and consistent use of Pgx open-source components.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. KLENT combines three well-established techniques (reverse-KL regularization as in MPO, entropy regularization as in SAC/SoftQ, λ-returns), and the analytic target in Eq. 3 follows from a standard Lagrangian derivation. The paper candidly locates its novelty in the empirical finding rather than the algorithm, but a reviewer must still weigh that the contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration that a known recipe transfers well to board games.

Evaluation relies heavily on win rate against a single anchored opponent (the Pgx baseline). A self-play agent can in principle overfit to one fixed opponent, and win rate vs. one anchor compresses the scale near saturation (KLENT's curves plateau around 80-90%). The supplementary head-to-head matches and Elo discussion mitigate this, but a proper round-robin evaluation across all trained checkpoints would substantially strengthen the central efficiency claim.

Only three random seeds per configuration, with no significance testing; several curves in Figures 5-8 and the ablation show overlapping confidence bands, making some per-game comparisons (e.g., versus TRPO AlphaZero in Animal Shogi/Gardner Chess) less decisive than the 'several-fold efficiency gain' headline suggests, which is largely driven by 9x9 Go, Hex, and Othello.

Some stability details of the value-learning scheme are under-specified or unexamined: the bootstrap estimate v̂ (Eq. 6) is computed from the same online networks used to generate data, with no target network, and the interaction between fitting πθ to π′ and then recomputing π′ from the updated Qθ is not analyzed. Whether the policy network contributes beyond distilling the Q-derived improved policy is not fully isolated in the ablation (the 'ENT Only' variant removes KL but keeps entropy; a variant that drops πθ entirely is not tested).

The budget metric (simulator evaluations) favors model-free methods in a way the paper acknowledges but does not quantify: AlphaZero incurs GPU forward passes per simulation whereas KLENT performs fewer network queries per sample. Wall-clock training comparisons are only briefly mentioned (25% reduction in one environment) rather than systematically reported for all five games.

The scalability result in 19x19 Go is the weakest part of the evaluation: only a single baseline (AlphaZero with tuned 16 rollouts), the strength is measured against the ELF OpenGo checkpoint at a point where both methods appear to saturate near 50%, and stronger recent baselines (e.g., Gumbel AlphaZero, KataGo-style training tricks) are not compared at this scale.

strengths: The central question—whether look-ahead search can be entirely eliminated for board-game RL—is clearly motivated and relevant given the well-documented computational cost of AlphaZero-style training.

The empirical evidence is unusually thorough for this domain: five games, three search-based and two model-free baselines, three random seeds, an ablation of all three components, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment.

The appendix addresses many potential objections proactively: AlphaZero rollout-count tuning (Table 5/6, showing KLENT still wins under the best rollout setting), wall-clock inference-time equivalence (Table 7), head-to-head matches against GnuGo and Pachi (Table 8), validation of the Pgx baseline against an independent AlphaZero implementation (Table 4), and a careful discussion of why Elo comparisons are unreliable.

The limitations section is honest: the authors explicitly state that efficiency gains do not imply superior asymptotic performance and that search-based methods may still win with massive compute—consistent with their own Appendix G.3 showing AlphaZero catches up at 3,200–4,000M evaluations.
The paper is generally well written and the algorithm (Eq. 3, Eq. 7, Algorithm 1) is specified precisely enough to reproduce, with all key hyperparameters unified across environments.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited. Reverse-KL regularization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns are all standard techniques, and the closed-form solution (Eq. 3) is a straightforward Lagrangian derivation. The authors themselves concede that 'the novelty of this study lies in our empirical result.' The combination resembles prior work (MPO, SAC, Grill et al. 2020, Sokota et al. 2022), and the delta from those papers (analytic target policy instead of PPO-style updates or replicator dynamics) is incremental.

There is essentially no theoretical analysis for the settings that matter. Self-play with an on-policy method in a nonstationary two-player zero-sum game raises well-known cycling and convergence concerns; the only theoretical support is a toy count-up game (Appendix L) showing convergence to a quantal response equilibrium, which does not establish behavior on real games.

Claims of generality outrun the evidence. The abstract and introduction position KLENT as broadly applicable ('discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, and mathematical proving'), but experiments cover only five small/medium games; in 19x19 Go the result is merely 'competitive' with AlphaZero rather than superior, and no non-board-game domain is tested.
Only three random seeds are used for the headline comparisons; given the noise visible in several curves (e.g., Animal Shogi, Hex), the margins in some games appear modest relative to seed variance.

The evaluation relies on a single fixed anchored opponent per game (Pgx checkpoints) for the main plots, which makes 'efficiency' claims sensitive to the choice of anchor; the head-to-head and Pachi results are reassuring but restricted to 9x9 Go.

The practical significance of 'simulator evaluations' as the efficiency metric, while defended, still favors the proposed method: search-based methods consume the same budget to obtain strictly better-backed training targets, so the fair wall-clock comparison is relegated to the appendix rather than foregrounded.

strengths: The central question — whether look-ahead search can be entirely eliminated for board-game RL while remaining efficient — is clearly motivated and well-scoped, and the paper convincingly answers it empirically.

Comprehensive and careful evaluation: five environments (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello), a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment, unified network architecture and hyperparameters across environments, and multiple seeds with variance reported.

The baseline treatment is unusually rigorous: Appendix F validates the Pgx AlphaZero implementation against an independent open-source implementation, Appendix G tunes AlphaZero's rollout count (a potentially unfair comparison otherwise), and Appendix H compares under equal test-time search and equal wall-clock time with measured inference times (Table 7).

Thorough ablation study (Fig. 6) with each component isolated via explicit hyperparameter configurations (Table 2), plus hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over 27 configurations (Fig. 9), and an empirical bias-variance analysis motivating λ-returns (Fig. 4).

Honest and substantive limitations discussion: the paper explicitly notes that efficiency gains do not imply superior asymptotic performance and does not claim search-based methods are invalidated (confirmed by Appendix G.3 showing AlphaZero catches up at 3,200–4,000M evaluations).

Useful supporting analyses: convergence to quantal response equilibrium on a small game (Appendix L), head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo/AlphaZero (Appendix I), and a careful, candid discussion of the pitfalls of Elo comparisons (Appendix J).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: reverse-KL + entropy regularization, the closed-form improved policy (Eq. 3), and λ-returns are all established techniques (MPO/Muesli, SAC, TD(λ)); the paper itself concedes that 'the novelty of this study lies in our empirical result.' The contribution is a well-executed combination rather than a new method or new understanding.

The framing of two-player games as single-agent MDPs glosses over the nonstationarity inherent in self-play; the theoretical grounding is thin, with the convergence claim (to QRE) validated only on a trivially small count-up game rather than analyzed for the actual algorithm.

Only three random seeds per experiment; given the variance visible in some curves (e.g., Animal Shogi KL Only, Gardner Chess), the evidence, while suggestive, is modest by ICML standards for strong claims of 'several-fold efficiency gains.'

The simulator-evaluation metric structurally favors model-free methods (each MCTS simulation counts as one evaluation), and while Appendix G mitigates this for 9x9 Go, the main-text search baselines use a fixed budget of 32 rollouts; the wall-clock advantage reported (25% in 9x9 Go, Appendix K) is considerably smaller than the 'fourfold efficiency gain' headline suggests.

Scalability of direct action-value learning to large action spaces is asserted as the key challenge (Section 4.2) but only tested on environments with at most ~1,225 actions; applicability to games with huge action spaces (e.g., full chess) or to the real-world MDP domains cited in the introduction remains speculative.

Some reproducibility gaps in the main text: buffer capacity, number of gradient steps, and schedule details are deferred to appendices; the description of 'stores improved policies in a replay buffer' (Appendix K) sits uneasily with the claimed strictly on-policy formulation.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive and careful: five board games plus 19x19 Go, ablations of all three claimed techniques, hyperparameter sensitivity (27 combinations), tuned AlphaZero rollout counts and extended training budgets (Appendix L), test-time scaling (Appendix M), head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo (Appendix N), wall-clock time measurements, and Elo caveats (Appendix O). The central 'up to 4x efficiency' claim is directly supported (Gumbel AlphaZero needs ~300M simulator evaluations vs 75M for KLENT to reach 50% average win rate).

The theoretical result in Theorem 5.1 / Corollary C.9 is a genuine, if modest, improvement: the local linear convergence condition alpha(alpha+2beta) > ||R||_2^2/4 strictly enlarges the guaranteed convergence region relative to Sokota et al. (2022), the proof via a weighted-norm Jacobian contraction is sound and clearly written, and the predicted boundary is validated numerically on Matching Pennies.

The paper is honest about its scope: it explicitly states that the contributions are not new algorithmic ingredients but new characterizations of a known combination, and the limitations section candidly notes that efficiency gains do not imply superior asymptotic performance with unlimited compute.

The ablations map cleanly onto the mechanistic claims: Figure 8 (KL divergence stays low with reverse-KL regularization) and Figure 9 (entropy collapse without entropy regularization) provide process-level evidence for the stability story, not just end-result win rates.

Reproducibility-relevant details are largely provided: full hyperparameters, unified network architecture (Appendix F), anchored opponent specifications, compute cost (~2,000 A100 GPU-hours), and memory analysis.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. Reverse-KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns are all standard, and the paper itself concedes no new algorithmic ingredients. The contribution rests on the empirical demonstration that this particular combination stabilizes self-play in board games, which is a useful but incremental finding; the improved convergence condition is a refinement of a prior workshop result (Sokota et al., 2022).

The finite-length-game theory (Theorem C.12) is informal relative to its normal-form counterpart. The proof assumes that 'after sufficiently many updates, Q_theta(s,a) has converged to Q^pi(s,a),' which glosses over the non-stationarity of self-play (Q^pi changes as the opponent policy changes) and the errors introduced by function approximation and lambda-return targets. As stated, the result is closer to a plausibility argument than a rigorous guarantee, and it does not cover the practical algorithm's replay buffer or function approximation.

Both theoretical settings are restrictive and only local: normal-form convergence is local around an already-existing fixed point, and the finite-length analysis relies on backward induction in acyclic games. Neither result directly explains why KLENT works in the deep, function-approximation setting where the empirical gains are claimed, leaving a theory-practice gap.

There is a possible concern with the framing of the test-time MCTS comparison (Table 2): KLENT is equipped with Gumbel AlphaZero MCTS at test time, so its strong 77.2% average reflects a hybrid train-free/test-search configuration rather than the pure model-free agent emphasized in the abstract, although Appendix M does separately show scaling without this conflation in the main curves.

No explicit code release is stated in the manuscript. Given that the paper's positioning is partly about reproducibility and compute-constrained practitioners (citing the 10 GPU-year cost of AlphaZero), releasing the implementation would substantially strengthen the contribution; the Pgx/Mctx dependencies help but are not sufficient alone.

The related-work positioning against stronger modern theory (e.g., Zhan et al. 2023's linear convergence results for regularized mirror descent, which the paper cites but does not quantitatively compare with) could be sharpened to better establish which parts of the convergence analysis are genuinely new.

strengths: The paper is unusually transparent about its contribution scope: the authors explicitly state that the algorithmic ingredients (reverse-KL + entropy regularization) are not new, and frame the contribution as a theoretical and empirical characterization of this combination in two-player games.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and unusually careful for this area: five board games, unified network architecture and hyperparameters across environments, tuned AlphaZero rollout counts (Appendix L), ablations of all three components, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, verification that the Pgx AlphaZero implementation is competitive against other implementations (Appendix K), head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo, Elo caveats, and wall-clock-time checks.

The result that a purely model-free method (KLENT) matches search-based methods at roughly 4-5x fewer simulator evaluations (and later matches AlphaZero's asymptotic 89% at 800M vs ~3,200-4,000M evaluations in 9x9 Go) is a meaningful and practically useful finding, supported by the Appendix L budget-extension experiments.

The theoretical claims are verified numerically: the convergence boundary in Theorem 5.1 (Fig. 3a) closely matches experimental convergence/divergence behavior (Fig. 3b), and the Count Up Game experiment in Section 5.2 exhibits the backward-propagation dynamics predicted by the proof.

Reproducibility is strong: implementation details (batch size, learning rate, threading model, network heads per method, Table 4), compute budget (~2,000 A100 GPU-hours), memory requirements, and sparse-buffer discussion are all provided.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific (efficiency-focused, no claim of superior asymptotic performance, finiteness/acyclicity assumption), and there is no discernible research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result for the practical setting (Theorem C.12) is not rigorous enough to support the claimed convergence guarantee for KLENT. The proof's induction step simply assumes 'after sufficiently many updates, the action-value estimate at that state converges to Q^pi' — i.e., it presumes the convergence of value learning, which is precisely the hard and unresolved part in the function-approximation setting where the practical algorithm operates. The result effectively holds only for exact tabular Q with a hand-waved value-learning assumption, leaving a substantial gap between the theory and the deep RL algorithm the paper actually evaluates.

The novelty relative to prior work is modest and the theoretical improvement over it is incremental. Sokota et al. (2022) already analyzed the KL + entropy regularization combination in two-player zero-sum games, including its convergence to quantal response equilibrium; the paper's improvement is a local linear convergence condition (α(α+2β) > ||R||²/4 vs. αβ > ||R||²) for a specific Jacobian-based analysis. Both results are local, and the experimental verification is on Matching Pennies and a 7-state synthetic game — settings too small to stress the theory.

There is a missing comparison to Muesli (Hessel et al., 2021), which the paper itself cites as the closest line of work ('reduce the amount of look-ahead search during training') and which is a model-free/policy-improvement method highly relevant to the central claim of efficient search-free self-play. Its absence from the main experiments weakens the 'pure model-free' framing.

The efficiency metric (simulator evaluations) structurally favors KLENT: search-based methods spend most of their simulator budget on rollouts per decision, whereas KLENT's cost is dominated by neural network computation that this axis does not capture. The wall-clock analysis in Appendix M/P partially addresses this but only for test-time inference, not for training-time wall-clock or GPU compute comparison, which is the actual resource claim in the introduction.

The experiments rely on only three random seeds per configuration, and several headline claims (e.g., KLENT > Gumbel AlphaZero average curves in Figure 5, the ENT-only gap in Figure 7) show overlapping standard-error bands in parts of the training range, making some efficiency comparisons less decisive than presented.

The empirical support for the two motivating mechanisms (gradual updates via reverse KL, exploration via entropy) is largely indirect: Figures 8 and 9 show that KL divergence is lower and entropy is higher with regularization, but the causal link from these observables to the performance differences is asserted rather than established (e.g., no intervention that decouples low KL from performance).

Presentation issues undermine polish: Figure 1 contains leftover draft artifacts ('Proposed Method (Motivation) 24' text overlapping the diagram), the proof in Appendix C.2 contains grammatical fragments, and minor inconsistencies exist (e.g., hyperparameters stated as (0.03, 0.1, e^{-1/8}) in Section 6.1 vs. (0.03, 0.1, ...) in Appendix F referencing Appendix E).

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: five board games plus a 19x19 Go experiment, unified network architectures and hyperparameters across environments, ablations for each component (KL reg, entropy reg, λ-returns), and unusually thorough appendices (rollout-count tuning for AlphaZero, architecture ablations, head-to-head matches vs. GnuGo/Pachi, wall-clock time, Elo, computational requirements).

The central empirical claim — a purely model-free agent that is up to ~4x more sample-efficient than search-based counterparts in games with large branching factors — is well supported, including fair test-time comparisons with unified compute and validation of baseline implementations against external references (alpha-zero-general, Pgx vs. Pachi).

Theory is verified empirically: Theorem 5.1's condition α(α+2β) > ||R||²/4 strictly improves over the αβ > ||R||² condition of Sokota et al. (2022), and Figure 3 shows the experimental convergence/divergence boundary matching the theoretical one; the Count Up Game experiments visually corroborate the backward-induction result.
The proofs (weighted-norm contraction argument, softmax Jacobian bounds, general-sum extension) are clean and technically careful.

The paper is honest about its positioning ('contributions do not lie in proposing entirely new algorithmic ingredients') and about limitations (efficiency, not asymptotic superiority, over search-based methods), which is commendable.
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation, hyperparameter, and hardware descriptions, with justification of the chosen AlphaZero baseline implementation (Pgx).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are modest relative to the empirical claims: both results concern the idealized update rule with exact Q-values, while the practical KLENT algorithm (neural Q-function, λ-returns, buffer sampling, self-play) has no theoretical support; Theorem 5.1 is only local convergence to a fixed point, and Theorem C.12's proof informally assumes Q-values 'converge after sufficiently many updates' without addressing the non-stationary two-player setting where Qπ itself changes.

Novelty is limited by the authors' own admission: reverse-KL + entropy regularized policy optimization is essentially MPO/Muesli-style mirror descent, and prior work (Vieillard et al. 2020a; Sokota et al. 2022; Zhan et al. 2023) already analyzed this combination; the main new contribution is the empirical demonstration in board games.

A direct comparison against the mirror-descent value-iteration method of Sokota et al. (2022) — which targets exactly this setting (QRE via mirror descent in two-player zero-sum games) — is missing; the 'ENT Only' ablation is close but not the same method, making it harder to isolate which ingredient drives the gains.

The improvement over Gumbel AlphaZero relies partly on a relatively shallow training-time search budget (32 rollouts per move); although Appendix L tunes rollout counts (best at 8) and extends AlphaZero's budget to 4,800M, AlphaZero does reach comparable asymptotic performance with more compute, so the advantage is confined to constrained budgets — the paper acknowledges this, but it narrows the significance.
Evaluation uses only three random seeds, and win rates against a single anchored opponent per game may under-represent the diversity of opponents along the learning trajectory.
Only the finite-action, essentially deterministic-transition setting is treated; extensions to stochastic and continuous domains (Appendices Q–R) are left as discussion rather than results.
